findings.title: First-run binding writes still use a fixed .tmp and can fail under concurrent startup
findings.preconditions: license bind_mode=first-run; 8-16 simultaneous processes sharing the binding path; local user
findings.summary: _write_binding_record uses binding.json.tmp / binding.json.anchor.tmp with no unique temp, no retry and no cross-process lock; 4 of 80 direct 16-process first-run attempts failed with WinError 32 / Permission denied. Full manage.py startup 16x5 did not reproduce, but the race window is real.
findings.root_cause: pyshield/runtime_template/_shield_runtime/_core.py:529-547 writes a deterministic path.name + '.tmp' then os.replace; _check_first_run_binding at :623-661 writes primary and anchor independently without _state_lock. pyshield/secure_store.py:179-212 already has the hardened mkstemp + retry logic but binding writes do not use it.
repro_steps: Extract PyShieldBuilder-protected-sample-round3.zip and derive the build key from _keyring.
Clear run/binding and set PYSHELD_BINDING_FILE to a fresh binding.json.
Start 16 binding_worker.py processes that each call _check_first_run_binding(build_key) once.
Observe intermittent LicenseError with WinError 32 or Permission denied on binding.json or binding.json.anchor.
findings.impact: Losing workers exit with LicenseError; retry recovers. A rare primary/anchor bound_at mismatch would leave 'bindings disagree' until both records are deleted. No plaintext recovery, machine-binding bypass or license forgery.
evidence: logs/binding-concurrency-sample.log: no .tmp leftovers; success-path records consistent
findings.remediation: Use secure_store.write_private (unique temp + retry) for binding records; hold _state_lock or a binding-specific lock across the whole read-modify-write; write both copies with one bound_at; add a 16-process x 10-round regression test.
findings.post_fix_verification: binding_concurrency.py with 16 workers x 10 rounds must report TOTAL_FAILURES 0 and no tmp leftovers; firstrun_concurrency.py must also remain 0.
findings.residual_risk: Anyone who can delete both binding records can still reset first-run binding; this is a known offline boundary.

findings.title: Legacy public-MAC migration is not one-time and can reset state mid-process while opt-in env is set
findings.preconditions: PYSHELD_ALLOW_LEGACY_STATE=1 is set by the deployment; attacker can write the state files; license expiry bypass additionally requires a system clock rollback (usually admin/root)
findings.summary: Default rejection of legacy public-MAC state is effective. However, the runtime accepts repeated legacy injections for as long as the env is set (no one-time marker); it also lets a writer bypass the in-process 'state disappeared' check by writing a legacy state.
findings.root_cause: _core.py:382-415 falls back to open_state(..., secret=None) whenever PYSHELD_ALLOW_LEGACY_STATE is truthy; _allow_legacy_state at :307-310 has no migration marker. _read_clock_locked at :470-500 re-seals keyed but never records that migration was done. Legacy MAC is a public SHA-256 (secure_store.state_key with secret=None), so no build key is needed to forge it.
repro_steps: Set PYSHELD_STATE_DIR to a fresh directory and write legacy-format clock state to both clock paths.
Call _check_clock(build_key) without the env: expect LicenseError.
Set PYSHELD_ALLOW_LEGACY_STATE=1 and call again: migration succeeds; both files become keyed.
Write legacy state again with the env still set and call again: it is accepted again (no one-time enforcement).
Start a process with _clock_started=True, delete both states (expect 'state disappeared'), write legacy state and set env; the next call succeeds and resets state.
findings.impact: With the env permanently enabled, a local state writer can repeatedly reset/rollback the clock state without the build key; combined with system clock rollback it can undermine expiry/rollback checks. The capability is close to the already accepted delete-both reset and does not directly recover plaintext or forge license signatures.
evidence: logs/legacy-state-tests.log: default_reject_legacy rejected; opt_in_migrate succeeded; opt_in_repeat succeeded again; future_keyed_30/future_legacy_30 rejected; future_keyed_1 accepted
mid-process test: after deleting both states -> 'clock state disappeared'; after writing legacy + env=1 -> accepted again
findings.remediation: Implement a real one-time migration marker or a one-shot CLI; reject legacy forever after the first successful migration; do not accept legacy while _clock_started is true; restrict last_seen to the accepted skew/range; add a regression test that a second legacy injection with env=1 fails.
findings.post_fix_verification: legacy_state_tests.py must show the first opt-in migration succeeds and every later legacy injection fails even with env=1; mid-process deletion plus legacy injection must remain LicenseError.
findings.residual_risk: The delete-both reset boundary cannot be eliminated in a fully offline client; keeping the opt-in env set reopens a public-MAC write path.

findings.title: Onefile rejection message recommends PYSHELD_BINDING_FILE even though the override cannot change the decision
findings.preconditions: onefile first-run license; operator follows the error message
findings.summary: The onefile guard is effective, but its error text suggests setting PYSHELD_BINDING_FILE to a persistent path. In a onefile process, _binding_paths_are_volatile returns True before looking at the override, so the suggestion cannot work.
findings.root_cause: _core.py:604-621 early-returns True when sys._MEIPASS is non-onedir, before consulting PYSHELD_BINDING_FILE; the message at :623-630 still lists PYSHELD_BINDING_FILE as an option.
repro_steps: Set sys._MEIPASS to a fake non-onedir directory.
Set PYSHELD_BINDING_FILE to a persistent path.
Call _binding_paths_are_volatile() -> True; _check_first_run_binding() -> LicenseError with the PYSHELD_BINDING_FILE suggestion.
Set sys._MEIPASS to sys.executable.parent (onedir) and repeat: the override is accepted.
findings.impact: No security bypass; the onefile app still fails closed. Operators may waste time setting an env that cannot help.
findings.remediation: Change the message to state that PYSHELD_BINDING_FILE cannot make a onefile binding persistent; recommend a fixed fingerprint or onedir. If onefile persistence is desired, implement and review a separate policy.
findings.post_fix_verification: binding_guard_tests.py should show an accurate onefile error message and unchanged onedir acceptance.
findings.residual_risk: First-run binding cannot be persistent inside a PyInstaller onefile extraction directory.

findings.title: Build-machine TEMP still contains many staging/CI copies; no sensitive values found
findings.summary: The high-sensitivity leftovers from round 3 (challenge source, diagnostic build secrets) are gone. 64 pyshield*/psh* TEMP entries remain, including old sample staging directories, CI HTML pages, a copy of the main exe and smoke directories; no new flag, challenge master/build key or real shield-secret file was found.
findings.root_cause: Ad-hoc mkdtemp/fixed-name build and test directories plus downloaded CI pages are not cleaned up; this is not a product vulnerability.
repro_steps: Only two 2-byte old.shield-secret.json test fixtures remain outside the pyshield* subtrees.
findings.impact: No sensitive data exposure was observed; old build/sample directories could still contain per-build keyrings if the machine is shared.
findings.remediation: Use TemporaryDirectory/finally cleanup; keep CI downloads in a dedicated workspace; add a release scan for flag, master/build key and *.shield-secret.json.
findings.post_fix_verification: Rerun temp_hygiene.py and confirm no matching sensitive hits and no real secret files.
findings.residual_risk: Same-machine users can always read TEMP; run sensitive builds under a dedicated account or machine.
